bugs: No WithoutOverlapping or other per-order lock. If a duplicate job ever exists for the same order, two runs can POST at once. Only the Idempotency-Key header (which assumes the partner honours it) stops a second shipment.
The Retry-After value has no upper limit (app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:141). A large header value can release the job past its one-hour retryUntil, so it fails with 'attempted too many times'.
If the partner keeps answering 429, the failure reason ops see is the generic 'attempted too many times' (confirmed by probe), not the 429.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:81: builds the URL by concatenating config('services.warehouse.url').'/shipments' instead of using Http::baseUrl().
app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:51-55: nested ifs where a single `&& !` condition would do.
app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:62: failed() calls refresh() on the job's own model and changes it in place.
tests/Feature/OrderShipmentTest.php:108-117: the mail-failure test works by forgetting the mail manager and adding an event listener that throws. It is brittle global-state manipulation.
strengths: Uses Laravel 13 queue attributes (#[Timeout, Backoff, MaxExceptions, DeleteWhenMissingModels]), the Foundation Queueable trait, #[Fillable] and enum casts.

Treats 422 as permanent: it records the reason directly and the job ends without retrying or failing. It handles 429 by releasing the job, honouring Retry-After. 5xx and connection errors throw so the backoff applies.
Claims shipment_notified_at with an atomic update before sending, and rolls it back if the mail fails, so the email goes out exactly once.
Dispatches with afterCommit in a transaction, applies the account-wide RateLimited middleware, and bounds retries by time with retryUntil.
Has a test that serialises and unserialises the queued job after the order is cancelled, which proves restoring the model does not ship a trashed order.

bugs: 429 is treated like a 5xx: it throws, counts towards MaxExceptions(8) and ignores Retry-After. A long rate-limit period therefore uses up the exception budget faster than necessary.
Every non-422 4xx (for example 401 from a bad token, or 400) is retried until the 8-exception limit, about 20 minutes, before ops see it (probe: a 401 left the order pending and the job retrying).
antipatterns: app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:58-64: checks shipment_status !== Sent twice in a row because createShipment returns void. Returning a bool, as impl-1 and impl-3 do, reads better.
app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:98: a 422 calls $this->fail(), which puts a business validation failure into failed_jobs as an exception.
tests/Feature/SendOrderToWarehouseTest.php:193-203: Mail::shouldReceive followed by forgetInstance and clearResolvedInstance is hacky facade resetting.
tests/Feature/SendOrderToWarehouseTest.php:211: calls the limiter closure with `new stdClass` to inspect configuration instead of testing behaviour.
strengths: The most idiomatic modern job: queue attributes, the Foundation Queueable trait, a typed retryUntil, and WithoutOverlapping plus account-wide RateLimited middleware.

handle() refreshes the order and checks trashed(), and #[DeleteWhenMissingModels] covers force-deleted orders. Probes through a real database queue worker confirmed a cancelled order is never shipped.
failed() reloads the order withTrashed and never overwrites a shipment that was already sent. When retries run out, ops see failed plus the HTTP error body (verified with a probe through the worker).
Atomically claims shipment_notified_at, with rollback, so the email is sent exactly once even across retries. Sends an Idempotency-Key header and uses separate connect and request timeouts for hangs.

Enum casts, #[Fillable], factory states paid() and shipped(). Tests use Http::preventStrayRequests, cover 429/5xx with a dataset, and cover recovery after an outage, a missing id and retrying only the mail.

bugs: notifyCustomer sends the mail first and only then saves shipment_notified_at (app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:145-147). If the save fails or the worker dies in between, the retry emails the customer again, which breaks the strict 'exactly once' requirement. impl-1 and impl-2 claim the flag first.
If the partner keeps answering 429, the order ends with the generic 'attempted too many times' reason instead of the 429.
antipatterns: app/Models/Order.php:19-27: string class constants for status and shipment_status instead of backed enums with casts.

app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:7-22: the legacy Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable and SerializesModels traits, and properties instead of Laravel 11+ Foundation\Queue\Queueable and queue attributes.
app/Models/Order.php:13: #[UseFactory] is redundant alongside HasFactory with a conventionally named factory.
app/Models/Order.php:66-69: after the conditional update, it hand-syncs model state with forceFill()->syncOriginal(), which is ceremony and leaves updated_at stale.
app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:26-33,60: more comments than the surrounding codebase, some of which narrate what the code does.
app/Jobs/SendOrderToWarehouse.php:97: uses forceFill although the attributes are fillable.
strengths: The most careful handling of partner responses: 429 releases the job and honours Retry-After capped at 120s, 5xx and 408 throw for backoff, and other 4xx and a 201 without an id are surfaced straight to ops.
markAsPaid claims the paid transition atomically with a conditional UPDATE, which is safe against racing webhooks and dispatches afterCommit.

handle() re-queries through the soft-delete scope and also checks the status is paid. recordFailure is guarded with whereNull('shipment_reference') and the soft-delete scope, so it never overwrites a sent order or touches a cancelled one.

The strongest tests: a behavioural rate-limit test with freezeTime and travel, an afterCommit rollback test against the database queue, withFakeQueueInteractions with assertReleased and assertNotFailed, and a global Http::preventStrayRequests.

v.rationale: All three suites pass (impl-2: 20 tests, impl-3: 24, impl-1: 25). Each implementation was also probed through a real database queue worker with queue:work --once, covering: an order cancelled after markAsPaid, a 422, a 503 then 429 then 201 recovery, a 503 until retries run out, a hang until retries run out, and a 401. All three are functionally solid. None of them shipped a cancelled order, all retried transient errors with backoff and recorded a failed status with a reason, and all emailed exactly once on recovery. The ranking therefore comes down to small robustness and idiom differences. impl-2 ranks first: it uses Laravel 13 job idioms throughout (attributes, Foundation Queueable, enums, #[Fillable]), guards against overlap per order as well as rate-limiting the whole account, refreshes the order and checks trashed(), claims the email atomically, and has a careful failed() handler. Its weaknesses are that it ignores Retry-After on 429 and retries non-422 4xx errors. impl-1 is almost as good and slightly simpler, with better 429 handling, but it has no per-order overlap lock and no upper limit on Retry-After. impl-3 has the most thorough handling of partner responses and the best tests (a behavioural rate-limit test and an afterCommit rollback test). It ranks last because of dated conventions (string constants, legacy job traits, a redundant UseFactory, comment-heavy code) and a real ordering flaw in the email step: it sends the mail before recording that it was sent, so a crash between the two causes a duplicate email.
